messages.content:
You are an evidence extraction specialist for PFAS treatment and remediation
research. Build a structured study evidence table before any narrative review
is written.

Extract one record per primary-study experiment, modeled scenario, or field
deployment that contributes usable evidence to the review task. A paper may
produce more than one record only when materially different matrices,
technologies, operating regimes, or endpoints would otherwise be conflated.

Review articles and perspectives may help identify terminology or primary
studies, but they must not be used as the source of a quantitative study
record. Never copy a review table as though it were a primary result.

For every populated source-dependent field:
- preserve the PFAS identity or class, matrix, starting concentration or
  loading, operating conditions, study scale, measured endpoint, value, unit,
  and material qualifiers when reported;
- attach only the field-level evidence locator identifiers that directly
  support that specific value or statement;
- use an empty string or empty array when the source does not report the
  information; do not infer or estimate it;
- do not turn the absence of information in the supplied packet into a study
  finding, quantitative result, or author-reported limitation unless the source
  explicitly states that absence;
- distinguish removal, separation, sorption, parent-compound loss,
  transformation, degradation, destruction, defluorination, mineralization,
  total organofluorine change, and toxicity change;
- classify endpoint_type from what was actually measured, not from the
  authors' preferred label. Parent loss alone is not destruction. Phase
  transfer is removal or separation, not degradation. Inorganic fluoride
  release or fluorine-balance closure can establish defluorination but cannot
  by itself establish mineralization. Use mineralization only when direct
  carbon-fate evidence such as CO2/inorganic-carbon production or a carbon
  balance is reported. Preserve a broader author term in reported_term and
  explain any mismatch in interpretation;
- do not normalize or compare values unless their units, denominators,
  matrices, PFAS scope, operating conditions, and endpoints permit it.

Only populate quantitative_findings when the source reports an actual numeric
value, inequality, approximate value, range, or explicit ND/not-detected
result. Put the number or censoring marker in value and the measurement unit in
unit. Normalize Unicode inequality signs to ASCII >= or <= and range dashes to
an ASCII hyphen while preserving the source wording in qualifiers. A unit or
order-of-magnitude scale without a number is not a quantitative finding.
Qualitative parent loss, intermediate formation, or disappearance belongs in
the endpoint interpretation or residual/byproduct statements instead.

Set value_form to exactly one of:
- exact_numeric: a bare number such as `99.7` or `1.2e-3`;
- approximate_numeric: `~` followed by a number;
- inequality: `<`, `<=`, `>`, or `>=` followed by a number;
- range: two numbers separated by `-` or `to`; or
- not_detected: exactly `ND`, `N/D`, `not detected`,
  `below detection limit`, or `below quantification limit`.

Put uncertainty, denominators, fold-change wording, and explanatory text in
qualifiers rather than value. A deterministic validator will remove malformed
quantitative fields before source verification.

For limitations, use basis=author_reported only when the source states the
limitation. Use basis=design_inferred only for a constraint that follows
directly from cited design evidence, such as one matrix, one compound, or
bench-scale operation. Never label missing information in the supplied packet
as a scientific limitation of the study.

Mark each record as comparable with conditions, descriptive only, or not
comparable. Comparability is an analyst inference rather than a quotation:
attach locators for the matrix, scale, conditions, endpoint, and denominator
on which the inference rests, and explain the reason. Do not reward a study
for reporting a larger percentage when its endpoint or conditions differ.

The task was derived from a defining review that is held out from all
candidate retrieval systems. The supplied anchor identifiers are an exclusion
list, not evidence. Do not extract from the anchor, cite it, reconstruct its
conclusions, or use its tables.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied evidence-table schema exactly.
Do not write the narrative review in this step.

records.citation: Vo, P.H.N.; Buckley, T.; Xu, X.; Nguyen, T.M.H.; Rudolph, V.; Shukla, P. Foam fractionation of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) in landfill leachate using different cosurfactants. Chemosphere. 2023;310:136869.

comparability.reason: Bench-scale foam fractionation applied to real landfill leachate with clearly described column geometry, operation mode, time scale, and qualitative performance (log removal ranges for long- and short-chain PFASs) provides evidence that is broadly comparable to other bench or pilot foam fractionation studies on PFAS-impacted waters, although differences in cosurfactant type, leachate chemistry, and operating conditions must be considered.

endpoints.interpretation: Foam fractionation transferred PFASs from landfill leachate into foamate, achieving 1.2–4 log separation for long-chain PFASs with all cosurfactants, and 1–2 log separation for some short-chain PFASs with cationic and zwitterionic cosurfactants; separation exploited PFAS sorption to air–water interface and cosurfactant–PFAS interactions.

PFAS adsorption at the air–water interface was characterized via interfacial sorption coefficients (Ki), spanning over four orders of magnitude and correlating with PFAS molar volume; Ki values were estimated by fitting first-order removal kinetics in the column.

PFAS concentration in leachate decreased over 0–60 min following first-order kinetics; long-chain PFAS residual concentrations were reported qualitatively as well below Australian Standard Leaching Procedure guideline values for PFOS+PFHxS and PFOA after treatment, but no exact residual concentrations were provided in the supplied text.
endpoints.reported_term: Removal kinetics and residual PFAS concentrations

limitations.statement: Results are based on a single bench-scale foam fractionation column configuration and landfill leachate matrix, which may limit direct extrapolation to other leachate chemistries or full-scale systems.

Quantitative performance is reported mainly as log removal ranges; detailed mass balances, recovery fractions, enrichment factors, energy use, and long-term operational stability are not documented in the supplied text.

operating_conditions.value: Batch mode with respect to PFAS removal; near steady-state continuous operation with respect to cosurfactant after initial stabilization

operating_conditions.value: Anionic, cationic, zwitterionic, and nonionic surfactants used as cosurfactants

operating_conditions.name: bubble_generation
operating_conditions.value: Recirculation through venturi mixer injector (0.5 inch) using centrifugal pump

operating_conditions.name: foamate_collection
operating_conditions.value: Foam skimmed via funnel 5 cm diameter positioned 10 cm above bulk liquid surface and pumped out; foam collapses to form PFAS-enriched foamate

operating_conditions.name: cosurfactant_feed
operating_conditions.qualifiers: Cosurfactant concentration in column builds up then equilibrates such that cosurfactant extracted in foam equals cosurfactant fed
operating_conditions.value: Continuous feed at constant rate during experiment

pfas_scope.value: Multiple PFAS species present in landfill leachate; both long-chain and short-chain PFASs including PFOS (C8), PFHxS (C6), PFOA (C7), PFBS (C4), PFPeS and others

quantitative_findings.name: long-chain_PFAS_separation_logs
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: All cosurfactants were effective for removal of long-chain PFASs, achieving 1.2–4 logs reduction in leachate concentration via foam fractionation.

quantitative_findings.name: short-chain_PFAS_separation_logs
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Cationic and zwitterionic cosurfactants recovered 1–2 logs of some short-chain PFASs (e.g., PFBS, PFPeS).

quantitative_findings.name: experimental_time_window
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: PFAS removal kinetics monitored over 0–60 min.

quantitative_findings.name: ASLP_limit_PFOS_PFHxS_sum
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Australian Standard Leaching Procedure (ASLP) limit for sum of PFOS (C8) and PFHxS (C6) in unlined landfill leachate; authors state long-chain residual concentrations were well below this value after foam fractionation.

quantitative_findings.name: ASLP_limit_PFOA
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: Australian Standard Leaching Procedure (ASLP) limit for PFOA (C7) in unlined landfill leachate; authors state residual PFOA concentrations were well below this value after foam fractionation.

residuals_byproducts.statement: Residual concentrations of longer-chain PFASs in treated leachate were reported qualitatively as well below Australian Standard Leaching Procedure limits for unlined landfills (0.07 ug/L for sum of PFOS and PFHxS and 0.56 ug/L for PFOA), but exact residual PFAS concentrations were not provided in the supplied text.
No information was provided in the supplied text on the composition or treatment of the PFAS-enriched foamate beyond its characterization as a concentrate produced for further treatment.

study_scale.value: Bench-scale foam fractionation column operated in batch mode for PFAS removal from landfill leachate

treatment.value: Foam fractionation using air bubbles and four different cosurfactants (anionic, cationic, zwitterionic, nonionic) to concentrate PFASs into foamate
